title: Interactive Cross-modal Learning for Text-3D Scene Retrieval

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims that IDeal "completely solves the alignment challenge" and achieves "near-perfect retrieval accuracy." The reported results are nowhere close to near-perfect: the best R@1 in Table 1 is 37.8 on ScanRefer, 26.4 on Nr3D, and 20.2 on Sr3D. The limitations section itself also states that "the performance of the methods is relatively low."

The manuscript invokes citation [60], even inserting a full reference-like entry in the body text: "Zhang, L., Wang, M., & Liu, Q. (2022). Bayesian Density Correction for Cross-Modal Retrieval. In Proceedings of ICLR 2022." However, the numbered References section ends at [59]; no reference [60] exists there. Thus the claimed theoretical foundation is not properly citable or verifiable from the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2.1, Density Compensated Factor and corrected similarity following Eq. (2)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claimed density correction has the opposite stated effect. The factor is rho(v_i)=1/(mean neighbor distance+epsilon), so dense regions with smaller neighbor distances receive larger rho. The proposed correction multiplies similarity by sqrt(rho(v_j)). For the positive similarities that determine nearest-neighbor retrieval, this increases, rather than reduces, scores in high-density regions. This contradicts the explicit claim that "high-density regions receive appropriately reduced similarity scores."

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2.2, feature fusion for Q1 responses
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The stated fusion equation is self-referential: "u_i^j = alpha u_i^j + (1-alpha)u_i^{j-1}." For alpha != 1, algebraically this implies u_i^j=u_i^{j-1}, so the new response contributes nothing. Presumably the right-hand u_i^j was intended to denote an unfused/raw feature with different notation, but as written the proposed refinement cannot perform the claimed weighted incorporation of new information.

Eq. (4) is not a minimum-enclosing-hypersphere formulation. A sphere constraint must involve a distance such as ||u_i^j-o_i|| <= R_i (or its square). Instead, the paper uses the scalar dot-product constraint "u_i^j o_i^T <= R_i." This neither defines containment in a sphere nor constrains a radius. In particular, choosing o_i=0 and R_i=0 satisfies all stated constraints, making the optimization degenerate rather than yielding a meaningful center and radius.

Eq. (7) defines a negative-log loss as -log S(tilde{u}_i,v_j), but elsewhere S is defined only as a similarity computation (Eq. (2)) and the actual normalized probability is separately denoted p or p-hat (Eq. (3)). Common similarities such as cosine similarity can be zero or negative, for which log S is undefined. No positivity transformation or normalization is specified, so this is not a valid negative-log likelihood as written.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.3, Eq. (9), weighted complementary contrastive loss
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The sign of the claimed negative-pair repulsion objective is reversed. For a valid similarity S<1, log(1-S) decreases as S increases. Therefore minimizing the stated term log(1-S) drives negative-pair similarity upward toward 1, attracting negatives rather than reducing their similarity/divergence risk. A repulsive loss would require the opposite sign (e.g., -log(1-S)) or an otherwise different optimization direction.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.3, Eq. (8) and its asserted upper-bound argument
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Eq. (8) does not define a mathematical upper bound: it writes sup(R_div(theta)) approximately equal to a brace-delimited pair consisting of an expectation and a variance. A scalar supremum cannot be equated to an unordered pair/set of statistics, and no inequality, scalar function of the mean/variance, assumptions, or derivation is given. Consequently it cannot justify Eq. (9) as an upper-bound surrogate for Eq. (6).

The same RoMa baseline is given materially different results for the same datasets and metrics without any stated change in protocol. For ScanRefer, Table 1 reports RoMa R@1/R@5/R@10 = 11.4/34.8/54.4, whereas Table 2 reports 9.7/33.1/50.2. For Nr3D, Table 1 gives 6.5/24.8/37.6 whereas Table 2 gives 8.3/27.9/37.2. Section 4.1 presents both tables as using the same experimental setting and does not explain these discrepancies.

The reported IDeal results are also inconsistent across the tables without an explained setup difference. Table 1 gives coarse-memory IDeal R@1 of 12.8 (ScanRefer) and 9.4 (Nr3D), while Table 2 gives RoMa+IDeal values of 16.0 and 11.7. Under fine memory, ScanRefer happens to match exactly at 37.8/71.8/86.4, strongly suggesting the rows are intended to be comparable, but Nr3D differs: Table 1 gives 26.4/62.7/78.7 versus 25.4/60.7/75.7 in Table 2. No distinction is provided that could reconcile the results.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 and all results marked with †
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The fine-grained-memory evaluation supplies the answerer with "fine-grained scene descriptions" and acknowledges "access to partial additional information." Since the answerer is supposed to answer about the unknown target scene, this constitutes target-scene privileged information/oracle memory unless a user independently possesses that exact information. These results cannot substantiate claims of practical retrieval from incomplete user queries, yet they are prominently used for the main best-performance claims. The paper does not separate oracle-assisted performance from a deployable protocol or quantify the amount and source of target information exposed.

Figure 4 is presented as IDeal R@1 versus interaction round, with the coarse-memory curve at about 15 on ScanRefer and about 11 on Nr3D at round 5. Table 1 reports the corresponding coarse-memory IDeal final R@1 as 12.8 and 9.4. No alternate model, split, or evaluation condition is stated for Figure 4, so the displayed round-5 values do not match the table's five-round setup.

The case illustration is internally malformed. It labels "Case 4" and then gives two separate "Round 5 Answer" entries with incompatible ranks, one ending "[Rank 4]" and another ending "[Rank 1]." The caption says Cases 1-2 and 3-4 are shown, but Case 3 is absent. As presented, the figure does not unambiguously identify which answer/rank belongs to which case or method.
